\chapter{Chapter05 — Hamming Ball Limit}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from FABL.Chapter05.HammingBallLimit
\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter05.HammingBallLimit}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Normalized Rademacher sum]
\lean{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p006-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p125-b003
}
\label{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.linearForm}
For a natural number $n$ and a sign vector $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, the normalized Rademacher
sum is the linear form in the coordinates of $x$ with every coefficient equal to
$1/\sqrt{n}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Hamming upper-tail indicator]
\lean{FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p006-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p125-b003
}
\label{FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum}
For a real number $t$, a natural number $n$, and a sign vector $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, define
the upper-tail indicator to be $1$ if the normalized Rademacher sum of $x$ is strictly
greater than $t$, and $0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Normalized Rademacher coefficient]
\lean{FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p006-b003}
\label{FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient}
\leanok
For a natural number $n$, define the normalized Rademacher coefficient to be
$1/\sqrt{n}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of the normalized coefficient]
\lean{FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient_nonneg}
\label{FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$, the coefficient $1/\sqrt n$ is nonnegative, with the
reciprocal interpreted as zero when $n=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Normalized sum as a linear form]
\lean{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum_eq_linearForm}
\label{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum_eq_linearForm}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.linearForm, FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$, the normalized Rademacher sum on $\{-1,1\}^n$ is the
linear form whose coefficients are all $1/\sqrt n$; that is, the two functions on the
cube are equal.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Permutation invariance of the normalized sign sum]
\lean{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum_permuteInput}
\label{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum_permuteInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.linearForm, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum, FABL.permuteInput, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$, every permutation $\pi$ of the $n$ coordinates, and every
sign vector $x\in\{−1,1\}^n$, the normalized sum of the coordinates of $x$ is unchanged
when the coordinates are permuted by $\pi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Negation of a sign value]
\lean{FABL.signValue_neg_hammingBall}
\label{FABL.signValue_neg_hammingBall}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
For every sign $s$, the real value of its negation is the negative of its real value.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Oddness of the normalized sum]
\lean{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum_neg}
\label{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum_neg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.linearForm, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum, FABL.signValue_neg_hammingBall}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$ and every sign vector $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, negating all
coordinates negates the normalized coordinate sum.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry of the upper-tail indicator]
\lean{FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator_isSymmetric}
\label{FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator_isSymmetric}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsSymmetric, FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum_permuteInput}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$ and real threshold $t$, the indicator of the event that the
normalized Rademacher sum on the $n$-dimensional sign cube exceeds $t$ is invariant
under every permutation of the coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sum of squared normalized Rademacher coefficients]
\lean{FABL.sum_normalizedRademacherCoefficient_sq}
\label{FABL.sum_normalizedRademacherCoefficient_sq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $m$, the sum over $m+1$ coordinates of the squares of the
coefficient $1/\sqrt{m+1}$ is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}
For every real threshold $t$, natural number $m$, and coordinate $i<m+1$, let
$R(x)=(m+1)^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_j$ on the sign cube of dimension $m+1$, and let
$H(x)=1$ if $R(x)>t$ and $H(x)=0$ otherwise. The Fourier coefficient of $H$ at $i$
equals $\mathbb{E}[H(x)R(x)]/\sqrt{m+1}$, with expectation under the uniform measure on
that cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier Weight of an Upper-Tail Indicator]
\lean{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_hammingUpperTailIndicator}
\label{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_hammingUpperTailIndicator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff_hammingUpperTailIndicator_singleton, FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel, FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_eq_sum_singleton, FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum}
\difficulty{3}
For every real threshold $t$ and every natural number $m$, let $A$ be the indicator on
the $(m+1)$-dimensional Boolean cube of the event that the normalized sum of its
coordinates exceeds $t$. Its level-one Fourier weight equals the square of the uniform
mean of the product of $A$ with that normalized sum.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Uniform measure on the sign cube]
\lean{FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure}
\label{FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.uniformPMF}
For a natural number $n$, define the Rademacher measure on the sign cube $\\{-1,1\\}^n$
to be the probability measure associated with the uniform distribution on that cube.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Rademacher coordinate summand]
\lean{FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummand}
\label{FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummand}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient, FABL.signValue}
For a natural number $n$, an index $i$ among the $n$ coordinates, and a point
$x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, define the coordinate summand to be the normalized Rademacher
coefficient in dimension $n$ multiplied by the sign of the $i$th coordinate of $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sum of normalized sign summands]
\lean{FABL.sum_hammingBallRademacherSummand}
\label{FABL.sum_hammingBallRademacherSummand}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummand, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$ and every sign vector $x$ of length $n$, the sum over
coordinates of the corresponding sign values, each scaled by $1/\\sqrt n$, equals the
linear form with every coefficient equal to $1/\\sqrt n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform Sign Measure as a Product Measure]
\lean{FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure_eq_pi}
\label{FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure_eq_pi}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure, FABL.uniformPMF, FABL.uniformSample_toMeasure_eq_pi}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$, the uniform probability measure on the sign cube of
dimension $n$ equals the product, over its coordinates, of the uniform probability
measure on $\{−1,1\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a uniform sign coordinate]
\lean{FABL.integral_hammingBallSignCoordinate_eq_zero}
\label{FABL.integral_hammingBallSignCoordinate_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.expect_monomial, FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure, FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.monomial, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{3}
For a natural number $n$ and a coordinate $i<n$, let $x$ be uniformly distributed among
all sign vectors in $\{-1,1\}^n$. The mean of the coordinate value $x_i$ is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a normalized sign summand]
\lean{FABL.integral_hammingBallRademacherSummand_eq_zero}
\label{FABL.integral_hammingBallRademacherSummand_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure, FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummand, FABL.integral_hammingBallSignCoordinate_eq_zero}
\difficulty{1}
For a natural number $n$ and a coordinate $i<n$, let $x$ be uniformly distributed among
all sign vectors in $\{-1,1\}^n$. The mean of the coordinate value $x_i$ multiplied by
$1/\sqrt n$ is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Independence of normalized coordinate signs]
\lean{FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummands_iIndep}
\label{FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummands_iIndep}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure, FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure_eq_pi, FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummand, FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient, FABL.signValue, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
For every $n\ge 0$, let $X$ be uniformly distributed on the sign cube $\{-1,1\}^n$. The
$n$ random variables $X_i/\sqrt n$, indexed by $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, are mutually
independent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integrability of a Normalized Rademacher Coordinate]
\lean{FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummand_memLp}
\label{FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummand_memLp}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure, FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummand, FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient, FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient_nonneg, FABL.signValue_eq_neg_one_or_one}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, coordinate $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and exponent
$p\in[0,\infty]$, the function on the sign cube given by the $i$th sign multiplied by
$1/\sqrt n$ belongs to $L^p$ for the uniform probability measure on that cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Variance of a normalized coordinate sign]
\lean{FABL.variance_hammingBallRademacherSummand}
\label{FABL.variance_hammingBallRademacherSummand}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure, FABL.hammingBallRademacherSummand, FABL.integral_hammingBallRademacherSummand_eq_zero, FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient, FABL.signValue_eq_neg_one_or_one}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$ and every coordinate $i$ among the $n$ coordinates,
consider a uniformly random point $X$ of the $n$-dimensional sign cube and the random
variable $Y=n^{-1/2}X_i$. Its variance is $n^{-1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform probability of an event]
\lean{FABL.hammingBallUniformMeasure_real_event}
\label{FABL.hammingBallUniformMeasure_real_event}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.hammingBallRademacherMeasure, FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.uniformProbability}
\difficulty{4}
For every $n\ge 0$ and every predicate $P$ on $\{-1,1\}^n$, the probability of the event
$\{x:P(x)\}$ under the uniform distribution on the sign cube equals the uniform
probability of $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Tail probability as an expectation]
\lean{FABL.expect_hammingUpperTailIndicator_eq_uniformProbability}
\label{FABL.expect_hammingUpperTailIndicator_eq_uniformProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum, FABL.uniformProbability}
\difficulty{1}
For every $t\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, the uniform expectation over the sign
cube of the indicator that the normalized Rademacher sum exceeds $t$ equals the uniform
probability of that event.
\end{theorem}

\leanok

\begin{theorem}[Vanishing normalized Rademacher coefficient]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_normalizedRademacherCoefficient_succ}
\label{FABL.tendsto_normalizedRademacherCoefficient_succ}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient}
\difficulty{3}
As the natural number $m$ tends to infinity, the sequence $(m+1)^{-1/2}$ tends to $0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Tendsto expect hamming upper tail indicator]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_expect_hammingUpperTailIndicator}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p125-b003}
\label{FABL.tendsto_expect_hammingUpperTailIndicator}
\leanok

\begin{theorem}[Mean of the normalized sign sum]
\lean{FABL.expect_normalizedRademacherSum_eq_zero}
\label{FABL.expect_normalizedRademacherSum_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.normalizedRademacherSum, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum_neg}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, the uniform average over $x\in\{−1,1\}^n$ of the
normalized coordinate sum $n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ is zero, with the coefficient
interpreted as zero when $n=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Positive Part Identity]
\lean{FABL.posPart_eq_self_add_neg_posPart}
\label{FABL.posPart_eq_self_add_neg_posPart}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For every real number $u$, its positive part satisfies $\max\{u,0\}=u+\max\{−u,0\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Reflection identity for stop loss]
\lean{FABL.expect_normalizedRademacherStopLoss_reflection}
\label{FABL.expect_normalizedRademacherStopLoss_reflection}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.expect_normalizedRademacherSum_eq_zero, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum_neg, FABL.posPart_eq_self_add_neg_posPart}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$ and every real number $t$, let $R_n$ be the normalized sum
of the $n$ coordinates of a uniformly chosen sign vector, namely
$R_n(x)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ (with the coefficient interpreted as zero when $n=0$).
Then
\[
\mathbb E_x[(R_n(x)-t)^+]=-t+\mathbb E_x[(R_n(x)+t)^+],
\]
where $z^+=\max(z,0)$ and the averages are uniform over the sign cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry of the standard Gaussian density]
\lean{FABL.gaussianPDFReal_zero_one_neg}
\label{FABL.gaussianPDFReal_zero_one_neg}
\leanok
\difficulty{1}
For every real number $t$, the standard Gaussian density has the same value at $t$ and
at $-t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Reflection identity for Gaussian stop loss]
\lean{FABL.standardGaussianStopLoss_reflection}
\label{FABL.standardGaussianStopLoss_reflection}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.gaussianPDFReal_zero_one_neg, FABL.standardGaussianStopLoss, FABL.standardGaussianStopLoss_eq, FABL.standardGaussianUpperTail_neg}
\difficulty{3}
For every real $t$, the standard Gaussian stop-loss function satisfies
$\mathbb{E}(Z-t)^+=-t+\mathbb{E}(Z+t)^+$, where $Z$ is standard Gaussian.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Stop-loss approximation for normalized Rademacher sums]
\lean{FABL.exists_normalizedRademacherStopLoss_bound}
\label{FABL.exists_normalizedRademacherStopLoss_bound}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.exists_stopLoss_linearForm_sub_standardGaussian_le_of_regular, FABL.expect_normalizedRademacherStopLoss_reflection, FABL.linearForm, FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient, FABL.normalizedRademacherCoefficient_nonneg, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum, FABL.standardGaussianStopLoss, FABL.standardGaussianStopLoss_reflection, FABL.sum_normalizedRademacherCoefficient_sq}
\difficulty{5}
There is a constant $C>0$ such that, for every natural number $m$ and every real
threshold $t$, the absolute difference between the expected positive part of a
normalized sum of $m+1$ independent uniform signs minus $t$ and the standard Gaussian
stop-loss value at $t$ is at most $C/\sqrt{m+1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Rademacher stop-loss limit]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_expect_normalizedRademacherStopLoss}
\label{FABL.tendsto_expect_normalizedRademacherStopLoss}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.exists_normalizedRademacherStopLoss_bound, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum, FABL.standardGaussianStopLoss, FABL.tendsto_normalizedRademacherCoefficient_succ}
\difficulty{3}
For every real $t$, the expectation over a uniformly random sign vector of dimension
$m+1$ of the positive part of the normalized Rademacher sum minus $t$ converges, as
$m\to\infty$, to the expected positive part of a standard Gaussian minus $t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Upper-tail indicator identity]
\lean{FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator_mul_normalizedRademacherSum}
\label{FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator_mul_normalizedRademacherSum}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, real threshold $t$, and point $x$ of the $n$-dimensional
sign cube, let $S$ be the normalized Rademacher sum at $x$ and let $I$ be $1$ if $S>t$
and $0$ otherwise. Then $IS=(	ext{the maximum of }S-t	ext{ and }0)+tI$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Tail-weighted sum identity]
\lean{FABL.expect_hammingUpperTailIndicator_mul_normalizedRademacherSum}
\label{FABL.expect_hammingUpperTailIndicator_mul_normalizedRademacherSum}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator, FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator_mul_normalizedRademacherSum, FABL.normalizedRademacherSum}
\difficulty{3}
For every $t\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, the uniform expectation of the normalized
Rademacher sum multiplied by the indicator that it exceeds $t$ is the sum of the uniform
expectation of its excess above $t$ (with negative values replaced by zero) and $t$
times the uniform expectation of that indicator.
\end{theorem}

  {context}

\proofstep
  {FABL.expect_hammingUpperTailIndicator_mul_normalizedRademacherSum}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p061-b007,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p125-b003}
For each real threshold $t$, the expectation over a uniformly random sign vector of
dimension $m+1$ of the normalized Rademacher sum multiplied by the indicator that the
sum exceeds $t$ converges, as $m\to\infty$, to the standard Gaussian density at $t$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
For each real $t$, take the indicator on the sign cube of dimension $m+1$ that equals
$1$ when the normalized sum of its coordinates exceeds $t$, and $0$ otherwise. As $m$
tends to infinity, the sum of the squared Fourier coefficients of this indicator over
all singleton coordinate sets tends to the square of the standard Gaussian density at
$t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Gaussian limits for a threshold on the sign cube]
\lean{FABL.proposition5_25}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p125-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p006-b003
}
\label{FABL.proposition5_25}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel, FABL.hammingUpperTailIndicator, FABL.standardGaussianUpperTail, FABL.tendsto_expect_hammingUpperTailIndicator, FABL.tendsto_fourierWeightAtLevel_one_hammingUpperTailIndicator}
\difficulty{1}
For every real $t$, let $X$ be uniform on the $m+1$ dimensional sign cube and set
$S_{m+1}(X)=(m+1)^{-1/2}\sum_{i=0}^{m}X_i$. As $m\to\infty$, the probability that
$S_{m+1}(X)>t$ converges to the standard Gaussian upper tail at $t$, and the total
squared Fourier weight of this threshold indicator on subsets of size one converges to
the square of the standard Gaussian density at $t$.
\end{theorem}
